summary: Extends OSPF to define independent IP topologies called Multi-Topologies. They can compute different paths for unicast, multicast, different classes of service, or an in-band management topology. An optional extension can exclude selected links. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: One city map can have separate maps for buses, bikes, and trucks. This lets a routing system keep different maps for different kinds of traffic.

subtitle: Lets OSPF keep several independent maps of the same network, so different traffic can take different paths.

tldr.problem: Standard OSPF computes one set of shortest paths, so unicast, multicast and other traffic classes all follow the same topology.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4915 reuses the old TOS metric fields in OSPF LSAs as a Multi-Topology ID (MT-ID), so each link and prefix can carry a separate metric per topology, and a separate SPF runs for each MT-ID.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run independent topologies for things like multicast or in-band management, and an optional mode can exclude links from the default topology. Migration from non-MT networks is supported.

today: RFC 4915 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2007. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reusing the TOS Fields
sections.content:
OSPF uses a fixed packet format, so backward-compatible extensions are hard. The RFC notes that the Type of Service (TOS) metric from RFC 1583 was never deployed and was deprecated. Multi-Topology (MT) routing reuses those TOS metric fields. They are renamed MT-ID and advertise separate metrics for each topology.

MT routing differs from TOS routing in three ways. It does not fix the topologies to the 16 TOS values, and how traffic is classified into a topology is outside its scope. Falling back to the default routing table for unreachable traffic is optional. And links or prefixes not advertised for a topology simply do not exist in that topology.

The abstract names the uses: different paths for unicast traffic, multicast traffic, different classes of service, or an in-band network management topology.
sections.eli5: OSPF already had unused boxes on its forms from an old idea. This RFC reuses those boxes so a router can write down a different cost for each kind of traffic.

sections.title: Terms and Key Ideas
sections.content:
The default topology is the one built from the TOS 0 metric. An MT topology is built from the metric for its MT-ID. An MT router has the capability; a non-MT router does not. An MT-Area contains both kinds of router or only MT routers, and a Non-MT-Area has only non-MT routers.

All MTs sharing a link must be in the same area, so area boundaries are the same for every topology, though each MT attaches to the area independently. A single adjacency is formed with each neighbor even if the interface participates in several topologies, and adjacency formation does not depend on which topologies are configured on either side.
sections.eli5: All the different maps cover the same neighborhoods. Two neighbors shake hands once, no matter how many maps they both use.

sections.title: Advertising and Computing Topologies
sections.content:
The TOS field becomes the MT-ID in Router-LSAs, Summary-LSAs and Type-5 and Type-7 AS-external-LSAs. Each MT has its own metric entry, and when a link is not part of a topology, that metric is left out. MT-ID metrics SHOULD be in ascending order of MT-ID, and if an MT-ID appears more than once, the first instance is used. Network-LSAs carry no MT information because the Designated Router is shared by all topologies.

OSPF runs a separate SPF calculation for each MT-ID, considering only that MT-ID's links and metrics. Network-LSAs are used by all topologies, and router routing table entries are MT-ID specific. When a link or prefix leaves a topology, a new LSA version MUST be originated without its metric for that topology. A router can also be made a stub in a topology by setting the maximum metric.

For prefixes to be reachable in a topology, a contiguous path inside that topology must exist. Forwarding, and how packets are associated with a topology, are out of scope but must be applied consistently across the network. For virtual links, the transit path and control packets MUST use the default topology.
sections.eli5: Each road sign lists a travel cost for each map, and a road missing from a map is simply closed for that kind of traffic. Each map gets its own shortest-route calculation.

sections.title: MT-ID Values
sections.content:
AS-external-LSAs use the high-order bit of the MT-ID field as the E-bit for the external metric type, so only MT-IDs from 0 to 127 are valid. Values 128 to 255 are invalid and SHOULD be ignored.

MT-ID 0 is reserved for the default topology, 1 for the default multicast topology, and 2 for IPv4 in-band management. Values 3 to 31 are reserved for IANA assignments and 32 to 127 for development, experimental and proprietary features. IANA created the registry "OSPF Multi-Topology ID Values" for these.
sections.eli5: Each map has a number. The first few numbers are saved for special maps, and some are kept free for experiments.

sections.title: Excluding Links from the Default Topology
sections.content:
A non-MT router treats the mandatory default metric field as valid even if it is zero, so it would wrongly keep a link in the default topology. An MT router therefore includes all links in the default topology unless it runs in DefaultExclusionCapability mode, a new per-area parameter that is disabled by default.

When enabled, the MT-bit (the old T-bit in the option field) MUST be set in Hello packets and SHOULD be set in Database Description packets, and Hellos without the MT-bit are discarded. Routers then form adjacencies only with routers that set the bit, which guarantees every router in the area supports exclusion. Routers advertise the default topology metric using MT-ID#0 and ignore the TOS 0 metric in Router-LSAs. Summary and AS-external LSAs still use the TOS 0 metric, set to infinity (0xFFFFFF) when the prefix is absent from the default topology.

Disabling the default topology on an interface only changes what the Router-LSA advertises, so OSPF packets can still use the link. Changing the mode needs extra care for demand circuits: Hello suppression must be disabled for RouterDeadInterval seconds.
sections.eli5: Old routers cannot understand that a road is missing from the main map. So the rule is to remove roads from the main map only when every router has promised it understands.

sections.title: Migration and Management
sections.content:
MT can be introduced gradually: MT routers share the default topology with non-MT routers and use other topologies among themselves. If links must be excluded from the default topology, all routers in the area MUST be in DefaultExclusionCapability mode. A new non-backbone area made only of MT routers may be set that way from the start. When several non-backbone areas use MT, the backbone area should be upgraded first, since inter-area routing still depends on it.

For management, the RFC suggests a dedicated in-band management topology containing all the nodes to be managed, with its routes optionally also installed in the default routing table. Alternatively the default topology can be extended to all nodes, with a high cost on the extended links so data traffic avoids them.
sections.eli5: You can add the new maps one town at a time. Old and new routers keep working together on the main map while the new ones also use the extra maps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no security issues beyond those already covered in OSPF itself (RFC 2328). It adds no new authentication or protection of its own.
sections.eli5: This change does not add new locks or new dangers beyond what OSPF already has.
